title: Baseline Serum Metabolites as Predictors of Teplizumab Response in Individuals With Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"We analyzed baseline serum samples from 41 individuals newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (T1D) enrolled in the Autoimmunity-blocking Antibody for Tolerance (AbATE) trial (NCT00129259) to identify metabolic predictors of teplizumab response. Responders to teplizumab were defined as individuals who exhibited <45% decline in baseline C-peptide levels at 2 years after start of treatment. We used a semitargeted metabolomics approach via liquid chromatography-high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry. We identified 15 significant (P < 0.05) metabolites, including amino acids and their derivatives, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates, and microbially derived metabolites. Responders exhibited higher levels of TCA cycle metabolites, amino acid derivatives, and microbial metabolites, whereas nonresponders showed elevated glutamate and acylcarnitines. These metabolites were used to train a supervised random forest (RF) model to predict treatment response. Model performance was evaluated using a 70:30 training-to-testing split, fivefold cross-validation, bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations), and permutation testing (1,000 permutations). The RF classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.769 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.881 in the test data set. These findings suggest baseline serum metabolomic signatures have the potential to predict responders to teplizumab with accuracy. This could potentially be applicable to other immunotherapies in T1D preventative efforts. Further validation of our findings is needed."},{"label":"ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS","text":"We believe that baseline serum metabolomic signatures can predict response to immunotherapies to identify which individuals will benefit most from treatment. We aimed to identify whether baseline serum metabolomic profiles can distinguish responders from nonresponders to teplizumab. Fifteen metabolites were identified as significantly different. Our findings suggest that baseline serum metabolomic signatures could be used to predict which newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes patients will respond to teplizumab, enabling more personalized treatment decisions."}]

title: Clinical Utility of a Type 1 Diabetes Genetic Risk Score Measured as Part of MODY Genetic Testing.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To evaluate the clinical utility of incorporating a type 1 diabetes genetic risk score (T1DGRS) into monogenic diabetes gene panel testing for individuals referred for suspected maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) from routine clinical practice."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We studied 1,129 individuals treated with insulin referred for MODY genetic testing. All underwent gene panel testing that included 10 variants to calculate T1DGRS. We compared T1DGRS distributions with reference populations to estimate the type 1 diabetes (T1D) prevalence within referred individuals. We defined age-specific T1DGRS thresholds to identify probable T1D (positive predictive value ≥80%) and applied them in individuals genetically unsolved MODY to assess its utility as a pregenetic testing triage tool."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"T1DGRS in MODY referral individuals was intermediate between reference populations with and without T1D, consistent with an estimated 20% (95% CI 14.9-25.2%) T1D in this real-world setting. After genetic testing, no excess T1DGRS was observed in individuals with genetically solved MODY, whereas those with unsolved MODY showed enrichment consistent with 26.0% T1D, with highest values in children (76.2%) and lowest in adults (16.8%). Age-specific T1DGRS thresholds identified 16.1% (95% CI 13.8-18.5%) of genetically unsolved MODY as probable T1D. As a pretesting tool, T1DGRS showed limited discrimination overall (area under the curve [AUC] 0.60) but performed well in children aged <10 years (AUC 0.83), where >50% of tests could be avoided without missing MODY."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS","text":"Incorporating a T1DGRS into routine MODY gene panel testing is feasible and clinically valuable. This approach broadens genomic diagnostics beyond monogenic disease by identifying T1D in individuals with genetically unsolved MODY. Pregenetic testing utility is age dependent and may reduce unnecessary testing in pediatric patients."}]

title: The Minimum Frequency of Well-Day Capillary Blood Ketone Testing Needed to Predict 1-Month Diabetic Ketoacidosis Risk in Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Independent of clinical risk factors, performing well-day capillary ketone monitoring over a month predicts near-term diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) risk. We aimed to determine the minimum frequency of tests needed to maintain similar accuracy."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"Using regression and machine-learning gradient-boosted tree (GBT) models on the Empagliflozin as Adjunctive to Insulin Therapy 2 (EASE-2) and EASE-3 trial repository (n = 1,410), we simulated the testing frequencies of capillary ketones over a 1-month interval for predicting DKA or severe ketosis in the next month."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Compared with the baseline twice-weekly ketone testing frequency, once-weekly well-day ketone testing was the lowest frequency that maintained prediction accuracy in maximum ketone models (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.692 vs. 0.678; P = 0.19) and GBT models (0.719 vs. 0.711; P = 0.38)."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS","text":"Weekly well-day capillary ketone testing, using existing strips before they expire, may provide a practical approach to stratify baseline DKA risk while reducing testing burden."}]

title: Single-cell profiling of pancreatic islets maps subtype-associated molecular alterations in type 2 diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Type 2 diabetes exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity, represented by distinct pathological subtypes. However, the precise molecular alterations underlying these subgroups at single-cell resolution remain poorly understood. In this study, we integrated clinical metadata from both healthy control groups and individuals with type 2 diabetes with pancreatic islet single-cell transcriptomes to explore subtype-associated molecular alterations across mild age-related diabetes (MARD), mild obesity-related diabetes (MOD), severe insulin-deficient diabetes (SIDD) and severe insulin-resistant diabetes (SIRD)."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"We applied the established type 2 diabetes clustering framework with independent validation against external centroids to evaluate subtype assignment accuracy across 43 pancreatic islet donors with type 2 diabetes. High-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing data comprising 131,083 cells from 32 pancreatic islet donors were subsequently analysed to systematically compare cellular composition and subtype-associated molecular perturbation patterns across these subgroups."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Four type 2 diabetes subgroups were identified, and validation against external centroids confirmed high assignment concordance, with subtype mapping sensitivities ranging from 85.0% to 100.0% in the full dataset and from 91.7% to 100.0% in the single-cell RNA sequencing sub-cohort. Notably, SIDD displayed the most pronounced beta cell perturbations, characterised by dual facets of beta cell dysfunction: the depletion of mature beta cell subclusters and the erosion of global cellular identity of beta cells. These alterations were accompanied by systematic activation of autophagy, apoptosis and endoplasmic reticulum stress pathways, while energy metabolism and insulin secretion were significantly compromised in SIDD individuals. In contrast, the SIRD phenotype manifested primarily as metabolic hyperactivation with largely preserved beta cell maturity. Additionally, MOD demonstrated moderate beta cell perturbations, characterised by enriched ribosomal function and protein synthesis activity. MARD displayed the mildest molecular disruption, consistent with its mild clinical phenotype."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"Our study provides an exploratory single-cell map of subtype-associated transcriptomic patterns in pancreatic islets across clinically defined type 2 diabetes subgroups. These findings serve as a valuable resource for future investigations exploring the cellular and molecular heterogeneity underlying type 2 diabetes pathogenesis."}]

title: Longitudinal Repeated Protein Measurements in a Multiethnic Cohort Identify Novel Diabetes Biomarkers That Reveal Unique Disease Pathways.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Circulating diabetes biomarkers have been identified with proteomics measured at a single time point, but what is additionally provided by longitudinal repeated measurements in the same individuals, over many years, is unknown. We studied participants in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA; n = 5,322; mean baseline age, 61.7 years) at exams 1 (2000-2002), 5 (2010-2012), and 6 (2016-2018) profiled with the Olink Explore (3 K) platform. Associations with incident diabetes, mostly of type 2, were modeled using Cox proportional hazards with exam 1 proteins (i.e., single time point) and time-updating Cox with proteins from all three exams (i.e., longitudinal repeated) adjusted for clinical risk factors. We identified 27 novel single time point associations and up to a fourfold increase in longitudinal associations (false discovery rate < 0.05), with a proportional increase in the number consistent with causality via cis-Mendelian randomization (∼5%) and a smaller overlap in MESA longitudinal versus single associations with UK Biobank single time point findings (42% vs. 87%, respectively). Compared with small-molecule metabolism pathway enrichment among the shared proteins, proteins unique to the longitudinal analyses enriched for protein and cellular processing pathways. We conclude that longitudinal repeated measurements identify a number of distinct disease biomarkers, in part by revealing the progression of relevant biological processes within an individual closer to a clinical diabetes diagnosis versus single measurements."},{"label":"ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS","text":"There is up to a fourfold increase in diabetes biomarkers identified with longitudinal repeated versus single time point proteomic measurements. The increase in biomarkers identified with longitudinal repeated measurements is supported by a similar proportion being nominated as causal for type 2 diabetes with Mendelian randomization. Proteins unique to the longitudinal repeated analyses highlighted biological pathways (e.g., posttranslational protein modification and cellular structure and cycle regulation) that were distinct from pathways enriched among the shared proteins (e.g., small-molecule metabolic and catabolic processes). Longitudinal protein measurements identify additional novel disease biomarkers and disparate biological pathways compared with single measurement analyses."}]

title: Differential physical activity responses to diabetes risk reduction interventions according to prediabetes phenotype in at-risk individuals: pooled analysis from three randomised controlled trials.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Emerging research suggests that the effects of lifestyle interventions to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes progression differ by prediabetes phenotype. We investigated whether this divergent effectiveness is accompanied by differing physical activity responses to the intervention."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Pooled data from three randomised controlled trials were used (n=2150), with up to 48 months annual follow-up. Participants at risk of type 2 diabetes were randomised to either: (1) usual care (control) or (2) similar interventions, in which they received structured group-based lifestyle interventions to promote increases in physical activity and other behaviours associated with diabetes risk reduction, supported by education, goal setting, pedometer use and maintenance support. Change in physical activity and glucose levels were stratified by the presence of impaired fasting glucose (IFG) and/or impaired glucose tolerance (IGT)."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Participants in the group with normoglycaemia were 63 years old (mean), with a mean BMI of 29.9 kg/m2; 56.4% were men and 76.7% were White European. Participants in the IFG group were 63 years old, with a BMI of 29.8 kg/m2; 70.0% were men and 79.1% were White European. Participants in the IGT group were 65 years old, with a BMI of 31.1 kg/m2; 60.4% were men and 80.5% were White European. Participants in the group with both IFG and IGT were 65 years old, with a BMI of 31.7 kg/m2; 62.7% were men and 82.6% were White European. The number of baseline steps/day was 6130 ± 3201 in the normoglycaemia group, 7244 ± 3489 in the IFG group, 5984 ± 2904 in the IGT group and 6310 ± 2872 in the IFG+IGT group (means ± SD). The intervention increased the mean number of steps/day relative to usual care by 247 (95% CI 4, 491) in the normoglycaemia group, 523 (95% CI 229, 818) in the IGT group, and 808 (95% CI 402, 1213) in the IFG+IGT group, but not in the IFG group (mean 71; 95% CI -429, 571). The intervention improved 2 h post-challenge glucose levels in the IFG+IGT group only (mean -0.5 mmol/l; 95% CI -0.9, 0.0)."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"The effectiveness of structured, group-based interventions with goal setting to promote physical activity differs by glycaemic status; those with IFG were least responsive. This may contribute to previously observed differences in the clinical effectiveness of diabetes prevention programmes."}]

title: Evolving phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a 15-year population-based comparison.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Our aim was to describe the phenotype at diagnosis and the early therapeutic profile of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes across two periods spanning approximately 15 years within the same integrated healthcare system."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"This retrospective cohort study used electronic health record data from Clalit Health Services (Haifa & Western Galilee, Israel). Adults with incident type 2 diabetes in 2005-2008 (period 1: n=80,201) were compared with those diagnosed in 2020-2023 (period 2: n=101,392). Between-period differences are presented as crude estimates, with an age-stratified sensitivity analysis, and quantified using standardised mean differences (SMDs; values ≥0.20 indicate at least a small effect) alongside non-parametric and χ2 tests."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"The median age at diagnosis increased from 63.0 to 66.7 years between the two periods; the proportion aged ≥85 years nearly doubled (from 3.5% to 6.6%). The score for the Charlson comorbidity index increased from 4 to 6 (SMD 0.48); metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) increased from 4.4% to 18.6%. HbA1c at diagnosis decreased from 56 to 53 mmol/mol (7.3% to 7.0%); pre-diagnosis LDL-cholesterol decreased from 2.90 to 2.21 mmol/l (SMD 0.65). Within 31-90 days of diagnosis, use of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors increased from 0.07% to 15.0%, use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) increased from 0% to 11.1%, and sulfonylurea use decreased more than fourfold (20.8% to 4.5%)."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"The phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes has been fundamentally restructured since 2008: patients are older with a higher comorbidity burden but present with better glycaemic and lipid management, with the latter reflecting statin therapy already established before diagnosis. MASLD has emerged as a major but largely ascertainment-driven comorbidity. The shift to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs alongside declining sulfonylurea use indicates displacement of glucose-centric strategies by a cardiorenal- and weight-driven paradigm. These findings indicate a need for age-appropriate management and trials enrolling very elderly patients."}]

title: Prediabetes subtype-based stratification reveals distinct long-term risks for type 2 diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Prediabetes is heterogeneous, with subtypes defined by impaired fasting glucose (IFG), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or HbA1c, each with different risks of progression to type 2 diabetes. We compared progression across these subtypes, and evaluated the benefit of adding insulin secretion and sensitivity to risk stratification."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"We analysed 7186 Korean adults aged 40-69 years from the community-based Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study, who were followed for up to 20 years with biennial (every 2 years) oral glucose tolerance tests and HbA1c. Prediabetes was classified as IFG, IGT or HbA1c-defined, and further stratified by insulinogenic index (IGI) and insulin sensitivity index (ISI). Cox regression was used to estimate diabetes risk, and multistate Markov models were used to assess annual transition probabilities and time spent in each state."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Compared with normoglycaemia, the adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were 5.84 (95% CI 5.03, 6.79) for IFG, 4.60 (95% CI 4.17, 5.07) for IGT, and 4.68 (95% CI 4.22, 5.19) for HbA1c-defined prediabetes. The risk increased stepwise with the number of criteria met: the aHRs were 3.10 (95% CI 2.81, 3.41) for one criterion, 7.33 (95% CI 6.50, 8.28) for two criteria, and 15.3 (95% CI 12.2, 19.3) for all three. Markov models showed the shortest prediabetes duration (1.7 years) and lowest regression probability (5.4%) in those meeting all three criteria. Low IGI or ISI predicted higher diabetes risk, and dual impairment conferred greatest risk (aHR 4.06; 95% CI 3.37, 4.90). Even normoglycaemic individuals with low IGI or ISI had an elevated risk of diabetes compared to those with high IGI or ISI."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"Diabetes progression differs based on both glycaemic subtype and physiological subtype. Integrating IGI and ISI with conventional definitions enhances risk stratification and may help to identify high-risk individuals for earlier targeted intervention."}]

title: Amino Acid Profiles Distinguish Glycemic Phenotypes in Childhood and Predict 10-Year Risk of Dysglycemia in Young Adults: The BCAMS Study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"","text":"Prospective evidence linking childhood amino acid (AA) dysregulation with future diabetes risk remains limited. We examined whether AA profiles distinguished childhood glycemic phenotypes and predicted dysglycemia risk in the Beijing Children and Adolescents Metabolic Syndrome (BCAMS) cohort. AA alterations were already detectable in children with normoglycemia and insulin resistance; six AAs were associated with 10-year dysglycemia risk, and their addition to clinical variables improved prediction. Ile showed the largest estimated indirect association with incident dysglycemia through follow-up insulin resistance; dietary Ile restriction in obese mice produced concordant metabolic changes, supporting AA profiling for early risk identification and Ile as a candidate modifiable target."}]

title: Predictors of Type 2 Diabetes Remission and Relapse After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery or Medical-Lifestyle Therapy in the ARMMS-T2D Study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Metabolic-bariatric surgery (MBS) is effective in promoting remission of type 2 diabetes, but this outcome is not universally achieved. We identified baseline patient characteristics that predict diabetes remission and subsequent relapse after various MBS procedures versus intensive medical-lifestyle intervention."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D) is a 14-year, multicenter study of health outcomes in 262 patients with type 2 diabetes (68% women, age 49.9 ± 8.3 years, BMI 36.4 ± 3.5 kg/m2, HbA1c 8.5 ± 1.5%) previously randomized to MBS (n = 166) or medical-lifestyle management (n = 96). Predictors of remission (defined as HbA1c <6.5% on no glucose-lowering medications) and relapse were determined using univariate time-to-event analyses of prespecified candidate predictors plus agnostic, multivariate least absolute shrinkage and selection operator."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Throughout a median of 11 years (maximum 14 years) of follow-up, 58% of participants randomized to MBS achieved diabetes remission versus 3% with medical-lifestyle management. Predictors of diabetes remission in univariate analyses included shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, fewer glucose-lowering medication classes used, greater body weight, higher fasting C-peptide and insulin levels, and weight loss at 1 year (all P < 0.05). Diabetes remission predictors in multivariate analyses included baseline diabetes duration, insulin use, and weight change at 1 year (all P < 0.01). Diabetes relapse after initial remission in the MBS group was predicted by longer baseline diabetes duration and greater number of glucose-lowering medication classes used."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS","text":"Baseline predictors of diabetes remission and subsequent relapse among participants randomized to one of three MBS procedures or a medical-lifestyle intervention should help inform personalized selection of diabetes treatment."}]

title: Clinical and metabolic subtypes of recent-onset adult type 1 diabetes: a prospective cohort study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"BACKGROUND","text":"Adult-onset type 1 diabetes exhibits substantial heterogeneity. We aimed to investigate whether this variability reflects distinct disease entities or different temporal stages of a shared autoimmune process."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"In this prospective cohort study, we analysed data from adults (aged 18-69 years) in the German Diabetes Study who had clinically diagnosed type 1 diabetes within the preceding 12 months, and from individuals who were positive for glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody (GADA) but had originally been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. We used unsupervised machine learning based on GADA status, fasting C-peptide, glucose, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol to characterise clinical and metabolic type 1 diabetes subtypes. The resulting subtypes were compared for aetiological traits (polygenic risk scores for type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes, partitioned type 2 diabetes polygenic risk scores, human leukocyte antigen [HLA] profiles, and islet-directed autoantibodies), insulin sensitivity, glucagon-stimulated C-peptide trajectories as a measure of residual β-cell function, and complications during prospective follow-up. Reproducibility was assessed in adults with type 1 diabetes from the German Diabetes Prospective Follow-up Registry (Diabetes-Patienten-Verlaufsdokumentation [DPV])."},{"label":"FINDINGS","text":"Analysed participants in the German Diabetes Study cohort were recruited between June 27, 2005, and Jan 20, 2025 (n=600), and were followed up for a mean of 6·1 (SD 4·7) years. We identified three type 1 diabetes subtypes: two GADA-positive subtypes, and one GADA-negative subtype. A similar clinical and metabolic subtype structure was observed in the DPV cohort, whose participants were recruited between 2000 and 2025 (n=483) and were followed up for a mean of 3·1 (SD 5·0) years. One GADA-positive subtype was characterised by lower BMI, higher insulin sensitivity, and severe β-cell dysfunction (classic type 1 diabetes), whereas the second showed higher BMI, lower insulin sensitivity, and better β-cell function (mixed type 1 diabetes). The two GADA-positive subtypes did not differ in autoimmunity or type 1 diabetes polygenic risk scores, whereas the GADA-negative subtype had lower genetic type 1 diabetes risk, despite no clear subtype-specific differences in HLA risk haplotypes. Longitudinal modelling indicated that the mixed type 1 diabetes group was positioned 6·1 years (95% CI 4·6-7·8) earlier along the β-cell function decline trajectory compared with the classic type 1 diabetes group. The risks of hypoglycaemia (log-rank p=0·0019), retinopathy (mixed type 1 diabetes vs classic type 1 diabetes: adjusted hazard ratio 4·93 [95% CI 1·71-14·24]), and cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (log-rank p=0·028) differed across the groups."},{"label":"INTERPRETATION","text":"Our results indicate that individuals with combined autoimmunity and lower insulin sensitivity present with clinical diabetes earlier than classic type 1 diabetes along the β-cell decline trajectory, identifying a potential timeframe for disease-modifying interventions in specific type 1 diabetes subtypes."},{"label":"FUNDING","text":"BreakthroughT1D, German Research Foundation (DFG), German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD), Schmutzler Stiftung, German Federal Ministry of Health, Ministry of Culture and Science of the State of North Rhine-Westphalia, and German Federal Ministry of Education and Research."},{"label":"TRANSLATION","text":"For the German translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section."}]

title: Targeting the ADA/ADO Axis Rescues β-Cell Failure in Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"The progressive decline of functional β-cell mass is a hallmark of type 2 diabetes (T2D), yet no current therapies effectively halt this process. While chronic inflammation and metabolic stress contribute to β-cell dysfunction, the key signals integrating these pathways remain elusive. Circulating adenosine deaminase (ADA) elevation in people with diabetes is often viewed as a bystander effect, not a pathogenic component. Here, we show that this elevation reflects a failed compensatory response in a previously unknown purinergic pathway linking dyslipidemia to β-cell failure. Circulating lipids trigger rapid ATP release from erythrocytes, converted to adenosine (ADO). Accumulated ADO drives tissue-specific ADA upregulation in organs affected by diabetes complications, including spleen, kidney, and islets. When this defense fails, toxic ADO selectively causes apoptosis in macrophages, podocytes, and β-cells via defined mechanisms. We show that exogenous ADA performs systemic clearance and local decompression, boosting circulatory adenosine clearance, normalizing tissue ADA hyperactivity, and rescuing islet immunopathology and function. These findings redefine a fundamental pathogenic circuit in T2D and establish the restoration of ADO homeostasis as a therapeutic strategy capable of producing functional β-cell recovery, thereby positioning disease remission as a mechanistically grounded and attainable goal."},{"label":"ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS","text":"Challenging the view that elevated circulating adenosine deaminase (ADA) is merely a secondary phenomenon, this study defines its pathogenic role in linking dyslipidemia to β-cell failure and establishes adenosine (ADO) homeostasis restoration as a disease-remitting therapy. We identify tissue-specific compensatory ADA upregulation that paradoxically fails to prevent systemic ADO accumulation, with elevated adenosine selectively inducing apoptosis in immune and pancreatic β-cells. We establish a novel systemic clearance-local decompression therapeutic mechanism in which exogenous ADA reduces circulating ADO, normalizes compensatory tissue ADA hyperactivity, and rescues islet function. This work redefines plasma ADA from a diagnostic marker to a therapeutic target, providing the rationale for an ADA-based therapy that uniquely combines immune modulation with metabolic correction to halt β-cell failure progression."}]

title: A Secular Increase in the Incidence of Islet Autoimmunity Among Colorado Children With Moderate-Risk HLA Genotypes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"We investigated islet autoimmunity (IA) incidence trends among Colorado children born 1993-2010 in Diabetes Autoimmunity Study in the Young (DAISY) and The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young (TEDDY) and whether HLA genotype or early-life environmental exposures contributed to observed increases."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We analyzed the risk of IA among 2,734 Colorado children representing three birth cohorts (BCs): BC1 (1993-1998), BC2 (1999-August 2004), and BC3 (September 2004-2010). Cox models evaluated IA by BC, with time-varying coefficients, BC-HLA interaction, and stratification by type 1 diabetes family history. Mediation analyses examined age at gluten introduction, weight-for-age Z-score, and maternal smoking."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"IA increased across BC1-BC3 (7.0%, 10.7%, and 12.7%). At age 1 year, moderate-risk HLA participants in BC2 and BC3 had, respectively, 2.57 and 6.19 times the IA risk of BC1. By age 5 years, effects attenuated. No selected environmental exposures mediated the increased incidence."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS","text":"IA increased among Colorado children born 1993-2010, with the strongest effects among moderate-risk HLA genotypes in later BCs."}]

title: Habituation to Elevated Glucose Levels in Type 1 Diabetes: Function and Well-being in Guideline-Based Versus Typical Glycemic Range.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Chronic hyperglycemia may shift physiological and perceptual thresholds upward, such that guideline-defined glucose targets feel aversive. We compared time in range (TIR) (70-180 mg/dL) with time in personal range (TIPR) (mean glucose ±50 mg/dL) to determine whether daily symptoms, functioning, and diabetes-specific outcomes align more closely with guideline-based versus personal glucose ranges."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"Adults with type 1 diabetes completed 14 days of blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), with ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) and mobile cognitive testing six times daily. For each 3-h interval preceding an EMA prompt, we calculated the percentage of time in guideline-defined and personal ranges. We estimated within-person correlations and regression models evaluating the incremental predictive effects of TIPR over TIR. Analyses were repeated stratified by personal (unblinded) CGM use."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Analyses included 161 participants (mean ± SD 41.1 ± 14.8 years old; 55% female; 41% Hispanic, 30% non-Hispanic White, 14% non-Hispanic Black). Compared with TIR, TIPR was more consistently associated with improved pain, fatigue, activity demands, and perceptual speed, whereas TIR was more strongly associated with better diabetes-specific self-evaluations (diabetes distress and self-care). Glucose metrics showed minimal associations with stress and negative affect, and TIPR showed modest associations with positive affect. In models including both predictors, TIPR explained unique variance beyond TIR for several outcomes. Associations between glucose metrics and diabetes-specific outcomes were stronger among CGM users than nonusers."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS","text":"Personal glucose ranges capture aspects of lived experience not fully reflected by guideline targets, supporting TIPR as a complementary metric for psychosocially informed, person-centered care."}]

title: 30-Year Trends in Microvascular Complications and Treatment in Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To examine trends in microvascular complications in adolescents from 1990 to 2019."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGNS AND METHODS","text":"Retinopathy, albuminuria, and peripheral and autonomic nerve function (pupil size and heart rate variability [HRV]) were assessed in 2,761 adolescents aged 12-20 years (duration ≥5 years) over 5,487 visits. Generalized estimating equations were used to examine the association between decades T1 (1990-1999), T2 (2000-2009), and T3 (2010-2019), and modifiable risk factors, including HbA1c variability, were assessed by coefficient of variation (CV)."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Retinopathy (T1 40%, T2 21%, T3 20%; P < 0.001) and early elevation of mean albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) (T1 35%, T2 29%, T3 28%; P = 0.009) plateaued and peripheral nerve abnormality rates decreased (T2 35%, T3 28%; P = 0.007), while HRV abnormality (T2 37%, T3 38%; P = 0.884) and albuminuria (T1 6%, T2 4%, T3 4%; P = 0.164) were unchanged. After adjusting for mean intrapersonal HbA1c, higher HbA1c CV was associated with early elevation of AER/ACR (1.27 [1.05-1.53; P = 0.015]), albuminuria (1.26 [1.04-1.52; P = 0.018]), and HRV abnormality (1.49 [1.08-2.05; P = 0.015])."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS","text":"Diabetes complications decreased then plateaued over time. These findings support lower glycemic targets, CSII use, and targeting of modifiable risk factors and HbA1c CV to reduce complications risk in youth with type 1 diabetes. The role of hybrid closed-loop therapy should be evaluated in the future."}]

title: Detectable C-Peptide and Diabetic Ketoacidosis Risk in Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To investigate whether detectable C-peptide levels in type 1 diabetes is associated with a lower risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We analyzed the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial publicly available data repository for the association between detectable stimulated C-peptide (>0.2 nmol/mL, measured annually) and DKA incidence over an average 6.5-year follow-up. We used crude and adjusted Andersen-Gill models for recurrent DKA events with time-dependent covariates."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Of the 1,441 participants (53% male, median age 27 years), 129 (9%) experienced 180 DKA events. Of these events, 179 (99.44%) occurred after C-peptide was ≤0.2 nmol/L in the prior year and only 1 event occurred with C-peptide >0.2 nmol/L. title: Developmental Control of DNA Damage Responses in α- and β-Cells Shapes the Selective β-Cell Susceptibility in Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Accumulation of DNA damage drives β-cell dysfunction, senescence, and death in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Although α-cell dysfunction also contributes to disease pathology, α-cells remain remarkably resistant to senescence and increased cell death under diabetogenic stress. The mechanisms underlying these differential responses to diabetogenic stress, particularly differences in their DNA damage vulnerability, remain unclear. We demonstrate that replication introduces a window of genomic vulnerability in both α- and β-cells during neonatal growth, with α-cells exhibiting higher replication rates and DNA damage. We show that neonatal β-cells resolve DNA damage more efficiently during mitosis and favor error-free repair, whereas α-cells compensate for their greater DNA-damage vulnerability through increased cellular turnover. title: Islet-Targeted ZnT8 Antibodies Protect Pancreatic β-Cells From Inflammatory Stress.

title: Dual Modulation of Prostaglandin E2 Receptors EP3 and EP4 Protects β-Cell Mass in a Model of Aggressive Autoimmune Inflammation.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Type 1 diabetes is driven by both β-cell dysfunction and an autoreactive immune system, resulting in β-cell destruction and hyperglycemia. title: Myeloid-Specific Heparanase Aggravates Insulitis in Type 1 Diabetes via Heparan Sulfate Fragment-Dependent Amplification of Macrophage Polarization.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"The intraislet heparan sulfate (HS) barrier is essential for β-cell survival, yet its role in type 1 diabetes (T1D) remains incompletely understood. title: Adipose Tissue Palmitoylation Cycling Mediates Insulin Resistance and Preservation of β-Cell Function in Mice.

title: Fecal Short-Chain Fatty Acids in Young Children and Their Mothers Are Not Associated With Progression to Islet Autoimmunity.

title: Islet Autoantibody Patterns Vary by Race and Ethnicity and Area Deprivation Index for Individuals at Risk for Type 1 Diabetes.

title: Adult Complications of Childhood-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Vary With Age at Diagnosis: A Population-Based Study.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Time-Restricted Eating in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

title: HGF Endogenously Produced by Pancreatic Pericytes Regulates β-Cell Function.

title: What Proportion of Antibody-Negative Type 1 Diabetes Cases Have a Nonautoimmune Etiology? A Genetics-Based Estimate.

title: Genetic association stratified by HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 status reveals heterogeneity in pathways of progression to type 1 diabetes.

title: β-Cell Dysfunction Identifies Individuals With Single Autoantibody Positivity at Increased Risk of Type 1 Diabetes Progression.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Individuals with single islet autoantibody positivity exhibit a highly variable risk for type 1 diabetes progression. title: Preserving beta cell function in children and adolescents with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes: per-protocol population analysis from the PROTECT randomised trial.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"In the PROTECT randomised trial, teplizumab demonstrated significantly greater beta cell function preservation vs placebo in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population. title: Harmine selectively enhances human beta cell identity markers and function via protein kinase A pathways.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Harmine and other small-molecule inhibitors of the kinase, dual tyrosine-regulated kinase 1A (DYRK1A), induce human beta cells to replicate and regenerate in vitro and in vivo and are effective at reversing diabetes in animal models. Harmine also rapidly enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in vitro and in vivo. These beta cell identity-enhancing effects are not due to DYRK1A inhibition. We hypothesise that they reflect interactions of harmine with a second target ('Target 2'). We aimed to identify Target 2."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"We performed an in-depth analysis of multiple different small-molecule inhibitors of DYRK1A in human pancreatic islets using gene expression, single-cell RNA-seq, proliferation, immunocytochemistry of beta cell transcription factors and identity markers, and solid-phase precipitation combined with proteomics."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"All small-molecule DYRK1A inhibitors studied (harmine, 2-2c, 5-IT, INDY, leucettine, CC-401, GNF4877) induced human beta cell proliferation via inhibition of DYRK1A. title: Shared non-HLA genetic architecture across diverse ancestries links insulin secretion and resistance to type 1 diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease with a strong genetic component. Nevertheless, the genetic underpinnings linking type 1 diabetes susceptibility to both insulin secretion and insulin resistance across diverse ancestries have yet to be fully characterised."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"We performed a multi-ancestry type 1 diabetes genome-wide association study meta-analysis comprising 26,198 cases and 36,733 control individuals to identify risk regions across diverse ancestral populations. We further evaluated their associations with clinical traits, integrated epigenetic profiles, mapped candidate genes to define tissue and cell type specificity, and conducted pathway enrichment analyses to elucidate the genetic links between type 1 diabetes and both insulin secretion and insulin resistance."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"We observed 69 non-HLA regions for type 1 diabetes risk, including three novel genome-wide association study signals: rs2179781 in AHI1 (OR 1.074, p=1.19×10-8), rs10117059 near TRAF1 (OR 1.074, p=3.95×10-8) and rs7184802 near ADCY7 (OR 1.089, p=4.12×10-8). Using Bayesian fine-mapping integrated with three complementary annotation strategies, we prioritised 136 putative functional variants. Integrative analysis leveraging Roadmap Epigenomics data revealed that these variants exhibited elevated regulatory potential, as evidenced by DNase I hypersensitivity, characteristic H3 histone modifications and active chromatin states in key metabolic tissues (pancreatic islets, liver, skeletal muscle and adipose). Subsequent functional characterisation identified ADCY7, regulated by functional variant rs1872691, as the probable causal gene at the novel 16q12.1 locus. In pancreatic beta cells, proinflammatory cytokines downregulated Adcy7 expression and Adcy7 perturbation bidirectionally modulated both insulin secretion and cytokine-induced apoptosis. Conversely, Adcy7 knockdown in adipocytes augmented lipogenesis and enhanced insulin sensitivity."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"Our findings support the existence of a shared non-HLA genetic architecture that may link type 1 diabetes susceptibility to both impaired insulin secretion and insulin resistance, providing preliminary genetic evidence for their convergent pathogenic mechanisms."}]

title: Delayed time to stage 3 type 1 diabetes after GAD-alum treatment in HLA-DR3-DQ2-positive children: follow-up of the randomised placebo-controlled Diabetes Prevention - Immune Tolerance trial.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"The aim of this study was to assess the long-term treatment effects of alum-formulated human recombinant GAD65 (GAD-alum) after completion of the Diabetes Prevention - Immune Tolerance (DiAPREV-IT) trial in 2017. NCT01122446), children 4-17.99 years old with GADA and at least one additional islet autoantibody were randomised 1:1 to receive two subcutaneous injections of 20 µg GAD-alum (n=25) or placebo (n=25), 30 days apart, with a 5 year follow-up. Both analyses were performed in the full population and in the subgroups with and without the HLA-DR3-DQ2 haplotype."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"After a median 12.9 years follow-up (range 1.0-13.8 years), 35 of 49 participants progressed to stage 3 type 1 diabetes. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01122446."}]

title: Microgels Containing Protease Resistant CXCL12 and FasL Enable Long-term Allo-Islet Function Without Systemic Immunosuppression.
abstract_json: [{"label":"","text":"Cotransplantation of allogeneic islets with microgels coated with streptavidin fused with Fas ligand and protease-resistant CXCL12 results in robust and sustained diabetes reversal for over 6 months in streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice and induces local immunomodulation, enhances Treg recruitment within the graft, and improves graft vascularization. This study addresses a critical challenge in cell transplantation, namely the need to develop technologies that enable local immunoprotection of the graft while eliminating the need for systemic immunosuppression. This combination microgel technology could offer a more favorable risk-benefit profile by reducing infection risks, organ toxicity, and tumorgenicity associated with the use of systemic immunosuppression. This novel combinatory immune modulatory approach is feasible and achieves anatomic site-specific immune protection while supporting long-term islet graft function without systemic immune suppression."}]

title: Increased Risk of Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Poor Sleep Quality Among Older Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The DCCT/EDIC Study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To investigate the prevalence of sleep problems and their risk factors among older adults with type 1 diabetes."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"Participants with type 1 diabetes in the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial/Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (DCCT/EDIC) study completed validated questionnaires to assess sleep-related problems, including risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) (intermediate/high risk: STOP-Bang ≥3), poor sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index >5), and mild or greater levels of excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale >10). Logistic regression models assessed the odds of each sleep problem by demographic and clinical variables, glycemia, and diabetes complications."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"In 963 participants (52% male, mean [SD] age 64 [7] years) with type 1 diabetes (mean [SD] duration 43 [5] years), diagnosed OSA and current positive airway pressure device use were reported by 29% and 19% of participants, respectively. title: Dynorphin A Inhibits Insulin Secretion Through Opioid Receptor-Dependent Modulation of β-Cell Ca2+ Dynamics.
abstract_json: [{"label":"","text":"The role of endogenous opioid signaling within pancreatic islets remains poorly defined. We investigated whether dynorphin A regulates insulin secretion and characterized the receptor requirements for the acute response to applied dynorphin A in mouse and human islets. Applied dynorphin A suppressed glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by remodeling β-cell Ca2+ oscillations through an opioid receptor-dependent, Na+/K+-ATPase-associated pathway. This response required μ-opioid receptors in mouse β-cells and was pharmacologically consistent with δ-opioid receptor involvement in human islets, defining species-dependent receptor mechanisms for the acute response to dynorphin A."}]

title: Efficacy and safety of low-dose IL-2 in people with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes (DIABIL-2): a double-blind, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial.
abstract_json: [{"label":"BACKGROUND","text":"Type 1 diabetes results from immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, driven partly by regulatory T-cell (Treg) insufficiency. We previously showed that low-dose interleukin-2 (IL-2) selectively activates Tregs in people with type 1 diabetes. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy of low-dose IL-2 in preserving residual pancreatic β-cell function and select an optimal regimen of administration in this patient population."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"This double-blind, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial was done in 19 academic hospital centres across Belgium, France, Germany, Switzerland, and the Netherlands. Both regimens started with an induction course of once per day subcutaneous injections for 5 consecutive days (days 1-5), then a maintenance course of injections (once per 2 weeks [regimen A] or once per week [regimen B]) from day 15 to 351. The primary endpoint was the change from baseline to month 12 in serum C-peptide area under the curve (AUC) from 0 to 120 min during a mixed meal tolerance test, analysed in the intention-to-treat population. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02411253 (completed)."},{"label":"FINDINGS","text":"Between June 18, 2015, and Nov 19, 2020, 159 people were assessed for eligibility, of whom 18 were ineligible and 141 were enrolled (48 randomly assigned to regimen A, 46 to regimen B, and 47 to placebo). 66 participants were in stratum 1 and 75 in stratum 2. 125 (89%) of 141 participants completed the study and 16 (11%) ended participation early. 54 (38%) participants were female and 87 (62%) were male. For log-transformed C-peptide AUC at month 12, there was no statistically significant difference in the overall population between placebo and IL-2 groups (geometric mean ratio 1·06 [95% CI 0·56 to 2·01]; p=0·85), with similar results when considering each regimen separately and by pubertal status. A marked Treg expansion was observed shortly after treatment initiation, peaking at day 5, with adjusted means of 1·31 (1·24 to 1·37) in the IL-2 group versus 1·04 (0·95 to 1·14) in the placebo group (difference -0·27 [-0·38 to -0·15]). Low-dose IL-2 was well tolerated across all age groups and treatment regimens. Nine (20%) of 46 participants in the placebo group and nine (10%) of 94 in the IL-2 group reported serious adverse events; one in each group was considered probably related to treatment."},{"label":"INTERPRETATION","text":"Despite robust Treg expansion confirming target engagement, low-dose IL-2 did not preserve β-cell function in people with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes. title: Adipocyte-derived exosomal ANGPTL2 promotes beta cell dysfunction via the EIF2α/ATF4/CHOP stress pathway in mice.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Obesity-associated lipotoxicity drives beta cell failure in type 2 diabetes, but the adipose-to-islet signals that promote beta cell dysfunction remain incompletely defined. We hypothesised that angiopoietin-like protein 2 (ANGPTL2) carried by lipotoxic adipocyte-derived exosomes contributes to adipose-to-islet signalling that impairs beta cell function."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Exosomes from palmitate- or PBS-treated 3T3-L1 adipocytes were applied to MIN6 cells and primary mouse islets to assess beta cell function and identity. In vivo, mice underwent adipose-specific Angptl2 knockdown under high-fat diet (HFD) feeding, followed by metabolic phenotyping and assessment of beta cell function. Adipose-derived exosomes from HFD-fed mice with or without adipose Angptl2 knockdown were injected into normal-chow-fed recipient mice, and endocrine marker composition and islet secretory function were evaluated. Angptl2 silencing in adipocytes lowered exosomal ANGPTL2 and mitigated islet dysfunction in vitro. Mechanistically, ANGPTL2 associated with eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α (EIF2α) and increased protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK)-associated EIF2α by approximately 2.8-fold, whereas this difference was lost after further normalisation to input EIF2α, supporting a substrate-availability model. PERK inhibition and integrated stress response inhibitor both attenuated ANGPTL2-induced activating transcription factor-4 (ATF4)/C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) signalling and improved GSIS."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"Lipotoxic adipocyte-derived exosomes increase ANGPTL2 abundance in recipient beta cells and contribute to beta cell dysfunction and identity disruption by amplifying PERK-dependent EIF2α/ATF4/CHOP signalling. title: BAF60A governs beta cell identity to control systemic glucose homeostasis.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Chromatin remodelling is critical for maintaining pancreatic beta cell identity and function, yet the key regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to investigate the role of the switch/sucrose non-fermentable (SWI/SNF) complex subunit BAF60A in preserving beta cell fate and glucose homeostasis."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Pdx1-Cre-mediated BAF60A-knockout (BaBKO) and BAF60A-overexpressing (BaBOE) mice, together with tamoxifen-inducible adult beta cell-specific Smarcd1 knockout (BaBKOTM) and Isl1 knockout (Isl1BKOTM) mice, were generated to evaluate the role of BAF60A in vivo. Multiomic analyses, including RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) and single-cell RNA-seq, were performed to characterise chromatin accessibility and transcriptional changes. BAF60A-interacting proteins were identified with biotin identification (BioID) and GST pull-down assays. Beta cell lineage tracing was used to assess changes in cell identity. BAF60A deficiency reduced enhancer accessibility and downregulated beta cell identity genes. Mechanistically, BAF60A physically interacts with the transcription factor islet-1 (ISL1) to regulate transcription of target genes. Adult beta cell-specific Isl1 deletion recapitulated key features of BAF60A deficiency and abolished the beneficial effect of BAF60A overexpression on insulin secretion. Conversely, BaBOE mice exhibited improved glucose tolerance and enhanced GSIS under high-fat diet conditions. Adeno-associated virus-mediated BAF60A overexpression markedly reduced beta cell dedifferentiation in BKS-db/db mice. In human type 2 diabetes islets, BAF60A expression was significantly reduced and inversely correlated with ALDH1A3."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"This work establishes BAF60A-ISL1-dependent chromatin remodelling as a key mechanism that preserves beta cell identity and function under metabolic stress, providing mechanistic insight into beta cell failure in type 2 diabetes."}]

title: Diabetes Care of Children With Type 1 Diabetes at School: Factors Related to the Choice of Care Location and Association With Glycemic Control.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Type 1 diabetes (T1D) management in children requires a comprehensive approach tailored to developmental stages and school environments. This study investigated the locations of self-management behaviors at school, examining factors influencing location choice and their associations with glycemic control."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"This multicenter, cross-sectional study analyzed 2018 registration data from 1,105 children with T1D attending schools or preschools in Japan. Care locations were the classroom (36.9%), designated rooms (52.6%), and the restroom (5.9%). HbA1c was significantly higher in the restroom group at 8.56% (0.98%) (70.1 [10.7] mmol/mol) than in the classroom group at 8.00% (1.20%) (63.9 [13.1] mmol/mol) and designated room group at 7.95% (1.08%) (63.4 [11.8] mmol/mol) (P < 0.001). title: Genetic background modulates MafAS64F-mediated islet ageing in male mice.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"In monogenic diabetes, there is increasing recognition that common polygenic factors can modulate diabetes penetrance beyond the causative mutation(s). CUT&RUN mapping revealed that MafA directly impacted expression of (at least) retinoic acid receptor-α (encoded by Rara) in islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice and circadian regulation in islets from mixed-background mice."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"In sum, these data show that genetic modifiers can impact beta cell regulation of retinoic acid signalling and circadian entrainment to modulate beta cell ageing and disease penetrance in mice modelling MAFA-MODY."},{"label":"DATA AVAILABILITY","text":"Sequencing data were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (accession no. GSE299343 for bulk RNA-seq and GSE298664 for CUT&RUN analyses)."}]

title: Glucose controls metallothionein 1 gene expression in pancreatic islets via a mechanism involving cellular metabolism, granular zinc and the zinc transporter ZnT8 in rat and mouse.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Metallothionein 1 (MT1) negatively regulates insulin secretion in pancreatic beta cells, and is upregulated by low non-stimulating glucose levels compared with physiological glucose stimulation in cultured rodent and human islets. Whether this regulation also occurs in vivo and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here we examine whether physiological changes in blood glucose levels in vivo control islet Mt1 gene expression similarly to ex vivo observations, and identify the mechanisms involved."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Rats fasted for 1, 2 or 3 days and rats fasted for 2 days and refed for 1 day were compared with rats fed throughout. Mice implanted with subcutaneous insulin mini-osmotic pumps were compared with control mice. Rat and mouse islets were cultured in the presence of optimal glucose levels (10 mmol/l; G10 medium) or low non-stimulating glucose levels (2 or 5 mmol/l; G2 or G5 medium) in the absence or presence of various modulators of mitochondrial metabolism, protein synthesis, Ca2+ influx, autophagy and insulin secretion. title: Contemporary Sex-Specific Mortality Risk in Type 1 Diabetes During the Era of Advanced Therapeutic Care.

title: Protective Effects of PD-L1-Overexpressing MSCs and Their Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"","text":"This study was conducted to address the urgent need for novel therapies for type 1 diabetes. title: Extracellular vesicles from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells protect grafted islets against endoplasmic reticulum stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction via modulating XBP1-based calcium homeostasis.

title: Associations of long-term exposure to air pollution with glucose homeostasis biomarkers and diabetes-related comorbidities in people with recent-onset type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

title: Cotransplantation With Human AAT-MSCs Enhances Human Islet Graft Survival in Humanized Mice by Modulating B- and T-Cell Responses.

title: Fetal, placental and amniotic fluid volume across gestation in women with type 1 diabetes: a prospective MRI study.

title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring Initiation Is Associated With Reduced Mortality in Older-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Patients: A Target Trial Emulation Study Within the Veterans Health Administration.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Use of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) improves glucose control and reduces hypoglycemia, but data are lacking for its possible role in reducing other serious clinical events."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We conducted a target trial emulation (TTE) analysis in patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) comparing all-cause mortality between CGM users and non-CGM users using observational health records from the Veterans Health Administration. title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring Metrics and Risks of Severe Hypoglycemia and Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Type 1 Diabetes: A Pooled Analysis.

title: Substrate-Selective Lipolysis Facilitates Unsaturated TAG Accumulation in Obesity.

title: Efficacy and safety of mazdutide in adults with obesity or overweight: a US-based, multicentre, phase 2, randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial.

title: Divergent complication patterns of type 2 diabetes in African individuals who are lean versus overweight or obese: a multi-cohort analysis.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Nearly 40% of African adults with type 2 diabetes are lean (BMI <25 kg/m2). title: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial of HTD1801 Monotherapy in Participants With Type 2 Diabetes.

title: The Effect of Obesity on the α-Cell Response to Hyperglycemia in the Presence of Amino Acids.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Hyperglycemia in prediabetes is accompanied by increased amino acid (AA) concentrations and impaired suppression of glucagon secretion by glucose. Therefore, lean participants and participants with obesity (with and without hepatic steatosis) were studied on two occasions in random order using a graded glucose infusion. Saline or an AA mixture was infused. The glucagon secretion rate (GSR) was derived from peripheral glucagon concentrations, and the change in glucose required to reduce GSR by 50% (G50) was calculated for each participant. AAs were measured during the experiment. On both occasions, experimental conditions produced a progressive rise in insulin secretion and an inverse exponential suppression of glucagon. G50 did not differ between groups in response to glucose alone. AA infusion did not change G50 in lean participants. G50 increased during AA infusion in participants with obesity with and without hepatic steatosis, leading us to report these participants as a single group. The relative change in AA concentrations across study days was generally similar between groups. We conclude that despite a normal response to glucose, obesity increases α-cell responses to AA in humans."},{"label":"ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS","text":"The aim of this study was to understand the pathogenesis of α-cell dysfunction in prediabetes. AA infusion impaired α-cell suppression in response to rising glucose in participants with obesity, but not in lean participants, despite a normal response to glucose alone. This abnormal response was unaffected by the presence or absence of hepatic steatosis. It seems likely that an abnormal α-cell response to AAs precedes an abnormal response to glucose alone."}]

title: Calorie-Restricted DASH, Carbohydrate-Restricted, and Low-Purine Diets for Weight Loss and Urate Control in Men With Overweight or Obesity and Hyperuricemia: A Randomized Trial.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To compare three calorie-restricted diets for weight loss, serum urate (SU) value, early urate dynamics, gout flares, adherence, and body composition in men with overweight or obesity and hyperuricemia."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"In this 12-week, open-label, active-comparator randomized trial, 102 men with overweight or obesity and hyperuricemia were assigned 1:1:1 to a carbohydrate-restricted diet (CRD), Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet, or low-purine balanced diet (LPBD). title: Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibition Attenuates Diet-Induced Obesity and Activates BAT Thermogenic Pathways Through Central Mechanisms.

title: Indices of obesity, malnutrition and inflammation are strong predictors of mortality in adults with type 2 diabetes: the FIELD study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Metabolic risk in type 2 diabetes is not fully captured by standard clinical measures. title: Reduction in T-Cell Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity After Reaching a Weight Loss Plateau.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Experiencing an involuntary weight loss plateau is common after behavioral weight loss. We studied mitochondrial respiratory capacity in peripheral mononuclear cell populations from participants with obesity, both before and after an intensive lifestyle intervention (ILI). Differences in mitochondrial respiration were observed in T cells but not in monocytes across these phases. During aWL, mitochondrial respiratory capacity was similar to pre-ILI; however, basal, ATP-linked, maximal, and spare respiratory capacity were significantly lower during the PL and RG phases. In addition, ATP-linked respiration was lower in the PL and RG, despite higher mitochondrial citrate synthase activity in the PL relative to pre-ILI. These results indicate that T-cell bioenergetics may be responsive to shifts in energy balance during weight reduction. The novel phase-specific classification used in this study uncovers dynamic bioenergetic adaptations that may contribute to a weight loss plateau."},{"label":"ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS","text":"Weight loss is a dynamic process, characterized by transitions between active weight loss, plateau, and regain, yet underlying metabolic features across these phases remain poorly defined. This study tested whether mitochondrial bioenergetics in peripheral mononuclear cells differ in humans across weight loss phases during behavioral weight loss. Mitochondrial respiratory capacity of T cells is significantly reduced during plateau and regain phases, despite an increase in mitochondrial content. Phase-based classification of weight change reveals bioenergetic differences in T cells that are associated with transitions in energy balance within the weight-reduced state."}]

title: Predictors of Peak Body Weight Loss With Semaglutide in the SELECT Trial.

title: Sphinganine as a novel stimulator of GLP-1 secretion.

title: Petrelintide, a human amylin analogue for the treatment of obesity (ZUPREME 1): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.

title: A Phase 2, Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Acmopatide (CT-868), a Fully Biased GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonist, in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes and Overweight or Obesity.

title: Efficacy and safety of oral orforglipron in Japanese participants with obesity disease (ATTAIN-J): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 trial.

title: FcRn Upregulation Exacerbates Podocyte Injury via Insulin Resistance-Induced Autophagy Disorder in Diabetic Kidney Disease.

title: Metabolomics-Defined Subtypes of Prediabetes and Risk of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Outcomes.

title: Association of Age at Type 1 Diabetes Onset With Survival, Cardiovascular, and Kidney Outcomes: A Nationwide Cohort Study.

title: Blood-Derived DNA Methylation Biomarkers Predict Diabetic Kidney Disease and Map to Epigenomic Remodeling in Renal Cells.
abstract_json: [{"label":"","text":"We undertook this study because albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate often identify diabetic kidney disease risk only after substantial kidney injury in type 1 diabetes. title: Renal tubule-specific Nrf2 deletion ameliorates diabetic kidney disease by attenuating glomerular hypertension and kidney injury in a mouse model of diabetes.

title: Accelerated Epigenetic Ageing in Diabetic Kidney Disease: A Comparison of 10 Epigenetic Clock Measures in Individuals With Type 1 Diabetes.

title: Novel Protein Biomarkers to Monitor Kidney Function Decline and Treatment Response in Individuals With Normoalbuminuria and Type 2 Diabetes.

title: Metadherin Drives FOXO3a Lactylation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction to Promote Podocyte Injury in Diabetic Kidney Disease.

title: Triphasic decline in kidney function after islet transplantation: sex-based differences and the impact of calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppression in a 20 year single-centre cohort.

title: Rsk4 Mediates Brain FGF19 Signaling to Constrain Diet-Induced Obesity in Mice.

title: Ketone Bodies Derived From Medium-Chain Triglycerides Support Brain Metabolism and Function Under Hypoglycemia in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.

title: Long-Acting RXR Agonism Preserves Retinal Function and Modulates Inflammation in Diabetic Retinopathy.

title: VDAC1 O-GlcNAcylation Promotes mtDNA Release and Activates ZBP1-Dependent Neuroinflammation in Diabetic Retinopathy.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a major cause of vision loss in working-age adults with diabetes. title: Deletion of 12/15-Lipoxygenase Preserves Retinal Thickness and Function and Selectively Restores Dysregulated miRNAs in Experimental Diabetes Mice.
abstract_json: [{"label":"UNLABELLED","text":"Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of blindness, characterized by progressive neurovascular dysfunction. title: The Joint Effects of Life's Essential 8 and Genetics on Mild Cognitive Impairment and Dementia Risk in People With Diabetes: Findings From the UK Biobank and All of Us.

title: Transient Cognitive Vulnerability After Hypoglycemia in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: Evidence From Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Cognitive Ecologic Momentary Assessment.

title: Effects of Pharmacological GIP Infusion on Insulin, Glucagon, and Cardiovascular Responses During Hyperglycemia in Type 2 Diabetes.

title: Early Weight Loss in Impaired Glucose Tolerance Is Associated With Reduced Long-term Mortality and Cardiovascular Risk: The Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Outcome Study.

title: Insulin Dosing Is Associated With Cardiac Sympathetic Predominance Independent of Glycemic Profiles in Type 1 Diabetes Under Free-Living Conditions.

title: Hepatic PDIA5 improves hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance through stabilisation of ATF6.

title: Unimolecular GLP-1/APJ receptor co-agonism improves metabolism and dyslipidaemia as well as normalising hepatic triglyceride and aminotransferase elevation in high-fat-fed mice.

title: Comparative hepatic effectiveness of empagliflozin vs dapagliflozin among individuals with type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

title: Prediabetes and diabetes as drivers of fibrosis in MASLD: roles of obesity, adipose tissue dysfunction and insulin resistance.

title: Genetic Susceptibility in Relative Maternal Protection From Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Type 1 diabetes is half as common in offspring of mothers versus fathers with type 1 diabetes. We investigated whether selective loss of fetuses with high genetic risk during type 1 diabetes pregnancy explains this relative protection."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"In 6,942 live births in The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young (TEDDY) cohort, we compared genetic susceptibility by family member with type 1 diabetes and tested whether it explained maternal protection from diabetes or its preclinical stages."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"The type 1 diabetes Genetic Risk Score 2 extended (GRS2x) did not differ between children with mothers (P = 0.36) or siblings (P = 0.27) versus fathers with type 1 diabetes. title: Skeletal Muscle DPT Ameliorates Obesity and Metabolic Dysfunction via the PERK/eIF2α/ATF4-GDF15 Axis.
abstract_json: [{"label":"","text":"We identified dermatopontin (DPT) as a previously unrecognized compensatory regulator that is upregulated in skeletal muscle in obesity and preserves muscle function and systemic metabolic homeostasis, offering a potential therapeutic target for metabolic disorders. title: Altered glucagon and GIP responses in South Asian versus Nordic women after gestational diabetes mellitus.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"We aimed to compare ethnic differences in levels of glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) following a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and to assess whether the higher insulin levels observed in South Asian compared with Nordic women could be explained by differences in the hormone secretory responses."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"We measured glucagon, GIP and GLP-1 in 178 South Asian and 107 Nordic women during an OGTT, and stratified participants by glycaemic status. GLP-1 responses did not differ between the ethnic groups (p=0.661). title: Low-Carbohydrate Diets, Nutritional Adequacy, Glycemia, and Perinatal Outcomes in Women With Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Secondary Analysis of the DiGest Trial.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"The optimal dietary carbohydrate intake for pregnant women is disputed internationally. Many authorities recommend a minimum of 175 g/day of carbohydrates primarily to support maternal brain glucose requirements and normal fetal brain development. title: A prospective controlled study assessing postpartum breastfeeding in women with type 2 diabetes: lower rates associated with elevated BMI rather than diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Breastfeeding is associated with metabolic benefits for women with type 2 diabetes and their infants, yet breastfeeding rates in these women are poorly described. The primary objective was to examine breastfeeding rates in women with type 2 diabetes compared with normoglycaemic women with either (1) matched BMI or (2) normal BMI. The secondary objective was to examine variables associated with breastfeeding."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Pregnant women with type 2 diabetes (cases) or normoglycaemia (controls) were prospectively recruited. Each case was matched with two controls by age and parity and either (1) matched or (2) normal (18-25 kg/m2) BMI. Analysis included descriptive and inferential statistics."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"Four months of breastfeeding data were available for 29 women with type 2 diabetes, 29 BMI-matched controls and 28 normal-BMI controls. title: Pregestational maternal diabetes primes neonatal beta cell dysfunction with structural remodelling, impaired calcium buffering and altered mTORC2-Gαq-PKCα signalling in a pig model.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Offspring of mothers with diabetes are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes, and this predisposition is established during fetal life. The aim of this study was to define the functional, morphological and molecular alterations in neonatal pancreatic islets associated with maternal hyperglycaemia, with a particular focus on beta cells, an area that remains poorly understood. Given its similarity to humans in endocrine pancreas development, the pig was used as a translational animal model."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Using genetically diabetic and beta cell reporter pig models, we performed functional assessments of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in vivo and in situ using fresh pancreatic tissue slices from neonatal piglets born to hyperglycaemic mothers (PHGs) or normoglycaemic mothers (PNGs). Morphological and molecular profiling, including proteomics and single-cell RNA-seq, were performed to elucidate molecular changes reflecting the developmental impact of maternal diabetes on offspring metabolic health, with a particular focus on neonatal beta cells."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"PHGs were born hyperglycaemic, hyperinsulinaemic and insulin resistant, exhibiting markedly delayed glucose and insulin response curves following oral glucose administration, with more pronounced effects in male piglets. In addition to an ATF4-dominated stress signature, a shift towards a distinct PHG beta cell subcluster characterised by low expression of ribosomal genes was observed, with an adaptive early-response-gene-mediated transcriptional reactivity. In contrast to the Gαs-adenylyl cyclase-cAMP-PKA signalling axis that dominated in PNG beta cells, neonatal PHG beta cells displayed distinct alterations in Gαq-PLC-PKCα signalling components, the mTORC2 target PKCα, and CREB1, suggesting a restructured signalling architecture."},{"label":"CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION","text":"Our findings reveal altered islet modelling with a unique beta cell dysfunction profile that partially overlaps with, but differs from, that of type 2 diabetes. title: Dual stimulation of Wnt and IFN-γ pathways in human bone marrow-derived multipotent stromal cells produces an activated secretome that modulates autoimmune diabetes in NOD mice.
abstract_json: [{"label":"AIMS/HYPOTHESIS","text":"Type 1 diabetes is characterised by continual autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells for which no curative therapy exists. Herein, we hypothesised that pharmacological licensing of MSCs with CHIR99021 and/or IFN-γ will generate conditioned media (CdM) with complementary regenerative and immunomodulatory properties. We also aimed to assess the modulation of autoimmune diabetes progression by licensed MSC CdM after intrapancreatic injection in NOD mice."},{"label":"METHODS","text":"Human bone marrow-derived MSCs were licensed with CHIR99021, IFN-γ or a combination of both, for 24 h, to generate concentrated CHIR, IFN-γ or COMBO CdM, for intrapancreatic (iPan) injection into female NOD mice and for label-free MS-based secretome analyses. These findings position MSC licensing and/or MSC CdM as an emerging therapeutic modality for the prevention of autoimmune destruction and regenerative medicine therapies for type 1 diabetes."}]

title: Life Course Cumulative BMI Burden From Childhood to Adulthood and Risk of Metabolic Multimorbidity: A 36-Year Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To examine the associations between cumulative BMI burden from childhood to adulthood and the risk of adult metabolic multimorbidity."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"This prospective cohort study used data from the Hanzhong Adolescent Hypertension Study (1987-2023). title: State Insulin Out-of-Pocket Cap Policies and Estimated Eligible Populations in the United States, 2019-2026.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"High insulin prices are a major barrier to diabetes management in the U.S. Since 2019, several states have implemented legislation to mitigate high out-of-pocket (OOP) costs for commercially insured individuals by setting caps on monthly OOP payments for insulin. We then estimated the number of commercially insured individuals using insulin still left unprotected due to 1) being enrolled in federally regulated plans, regardless of state of residence, or 2) being enrolled in state-regulated plans but living in states without OOP cap legislation."},{"label":"RESULTS","text":"By 2026, 29 states and Washington, DC, had enacted OOP caps on insulin, covering an estimated 0.99 million individuals with diabetes, using insulin, and enrolled in state-regulated commercial plans. title: Multiple 24-Hour Urinary Sodium and Potassium Excretions and Type 2 Diabetes Incidence.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"High sodium and low potassium intake, well-established dietary risk factors for hypertension, may induce insulin resistance and increase the risk of type 2 diabetes. We examined the association of sodium and potassium intake, assessed by multiple 24-h urine samples, with subsequent risk of developing type 2 diabetes."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We included 3,173 adults without major chronic diseases from three prospective cohorts. Each 1,000 mg/day increase in sodium excretion was associated with a 32% (HR 1.32; 95% CI 1.16-1.52) higher risk of diabetes, whereas potassium excretion was not associated with diabetes risk (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.69-1.11). title: Emergency Hospitalization, Amputation, and Survival After Charcot Neuro-Osteoarthropathy Diagnosis in People With Diabetes: A Regional Registry-Based Cohort Study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"The aim for this study was to describe adverse outcomes after Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy (CNO) diagnosis in adults with diabetes and examine variation by clinical and sociodemographic characteristics."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"A regional, registry-based cohort study was conducted using linked routinely collected health care data from adults with diabetes and a first recorded CNO diagnosis in the National Health Service Greater Glasgow and Clyde, Scotland (2015-2024). These findings support CNO as a marker of systemic vulnerability and highlight the need for prioritized surveillance and multidisciplinary management in routine clinical care."}]

title: Housing Instability Associated With Cost-Related Nonadherence and Financial Toxicity in People With Uncontrolled Diabetes.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"To assess the prevalence of housing instability and its associations with cost-related nonadherence and financial toxicity among adults with uncontrolled diabetes."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We analyzed baseline randomized controlled trial data from 600 adults with uncontrolled diabetes and cost-related barriers to care. title: Excess Burden of Inpatient Admissions and Emergency Department Visits Associated With Diabetes Across the Age Spectrum.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"The epidemiology of diabetes and its complications is changing due to increasingly younger ages of diagnosis and increased life expectancy. How this changing landscape affects health care use, and for which conditions, is unclear. We examined age-specific excess burdens of cause-specific inpatient and emergency department (ED) visits associated with diabetes."},{"label":"RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS","text":"We used 2019 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, National Inpatient Sample, and Nationwide Emergency Department Sample data to derive national U.S. estimates of inpatient admissions and ED visits in adults with and without diabetes. title: All-Cause Mortality, Morbidity, and Reamputation Rates Following Below-Knee Amputation in 25,176 People With Diabetes: A 25-Year England Population Study.
abstract_json: [{"label":"OBJECTIVE","text":"Below-knee amputation (BKA) is the most common major amputation for advanced diabetic foot disease. Understanding the associated mortality, cause of death, and postoperative risks is important for patient counseling and improving care. This national population study described mortality and causes of death following BKA in people with diabetes, identifying those at greatest risk and whether mortality has improved.
